hints: Look at the first and last characters of s. If they are the same, they can be the outer pair of the mirror. If they differ, one of them cannot be in the answer at all.
Interval DP: dp[i][j] = longest mirror (palindromic subsequence) hidden inside s[i..j]. Fill it for shorter ranges first (i from right to left, j from i to the end).

1. Every single character is a mirror of length 1: dp[i][i] = 1.
  2. Loop i from n-1 down to 0, and j from i+1 up to n-1.
  3. If s[i] == s[j]: dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2 (inner part may be empty → 0).
  4. Else: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
  5. Return dp[0][n-1].

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try all 2<sup>n</sup> subsequences, check which are palindromes, keep the longest.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Interval DP over substrings using the match-the-ends rule. (Equivalent: LCS of s and its reverse.)

explain: For "character", the outer letters c and r differ, so the answer is the better of dropping the first or the last letter. Deeper in, ranges whose ends match (like c…c and a…a) add 2 to their inside, building up "carac" of length 5. The invariant is that dp[i][j] is already correct for every shorter range when we compute it, because i goes downward and j goes upward. Edge case: when j = i+1 and the two letters match, the inside is empty, so it should count as 0, giving 2.
recognize: 'Delete characters so what remains reads the same both ways' on one string → interval DP on s[i..j] with matching ends.
